detailed_rationale:
Aavas Financiers is a granular, retail-focused affordable-housing-finance NBFC-HFC serving first-time homebuyers and self-employed borrowers in semi-urban and rural India. As a financial-services lender, the D/E of 3.11x on the quant screen is a normal function of the business model (borrowed funds relent as housing loans), not a distress signal, and is judged here on asset quality and growth instead per the standard financial-sector exemption.

Q1 FY27 (Jun-2026 quarter) results were strong on every operating metric that matters for an HFC: AUM grew 15.4% YoY to roughly Rs 23,930 crore, disbursements grew 41% YoY, and net profit rose 23% YoY to about Rs 171 crore, aided by 18% YoY NII growth and improving operating efficiency. Asset quality, already a long-standing Aavas strength, improved further: 1+ DPD fell 39 bps YoY to 3.76% and net Stage III (net NPA) improved to 0.71%, with gross NPA down 11 bps YoY. Management guided FY27 AUM growth of 17-18% and disbursement growth of 22-23%, both consistent with the current run-rate.

The company has also been through a full change of promoter within the last two years: private-equity sponsors Partners Group and Kedaara Capital fully exited (Partners Group's final exit was to CVC Capital in mid-2025), with a CVC-linked entity subsequently emerging as the new promoter via an open offer. This is a PE-to-PE ownership handover rather than a strategic or distressed change of control, and the operating numbers show no disruption through the transition -- management (CEO Sachinder Bhardwaj) has continued, and growth/asset-quality metrics have if anything improved through the period. Valuation has compressed to 18.1x trailing earnings, modest for an HFC compounding AUM at mid-to-high teens with sub-1% net NPAs.
recommendation_rationale: The quant Sell is being driven by valuation/momentum-type sub-scores rather than a fundamental problem -- on the metrics that actually matter for a housing financier (AUM growth, disbursement growth, asset quality, ROE), Aavas is executing well and improving, and the stock has simply de-rated to a more reasonable multiple (18x) after a period of much richer valuations. I am rescuing this to Hold on the strength of the AUM/asset-quality trend; I am not calling it a high-conviction re-rating case given the recent full promoter change is still a relatively fresh development worth continuing to monitor.
summary: Aavas is an affordable-housing lender that continues to grow its loan book at a healthy mid-teens pace while keeping bad-loan levels among the lowest in its peer group, and its most recent quarter showed profit growth accelerating. The company went through a full change of controlling shareholder over the last two years (one private-equity owner selling to another), but the day-to-day business has kept performing well through that transition. Given the strong growth and asset quality trend and a valuation that is no longer expensive, we view this as a hold.
positive_para: Aavas continues to deliver what a granular housing financier should: AUM up 15.4% YoY, disbursements up a strong 41% YoY, and asset quality that keeps improving rather than deteriorating (net Stage III down to 0.71%). Management's FY27 guidance of 17-18% AUM growth is consistent with the current trend, and at 18.1x trailing earnings the stock is no longer pricing in aggressive growth assumptions the way it once did.
negative_para: The company underwent a full promoter change within roughly the last two years, with private-equity sponsors selling out entirely and a new CVC-linked promoter (Aquilo House) emerging via an open offer -- this kind of ownership discontinuity, even when financially clean, is worth watching for any shift in underwriting discipline, growth appetite, or capital-allocation priorities under new ownership, since the track record with the new controlling shareholder is still short. The 3.11x leverage is normal for the HFC model, but it does mean asset-quality slippage would flow through to earnings quickly if the underwriting discipline that has driven the low NPA ratios to date were to loosen.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At 18.1x trailing earnings for an HFC compounding AUM in the mid-to-high teens with sub-1% net NPAs and 13% ROE, the multiple is not demanding -- it implies the market is pricing continuity of the current growth/asset-quality trend rather than acceleration or a re-rating. That looks achievable given the FY27 guidance and recent execution, making this closer to fairly valued than expensive.
